title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without the rights holders' authorisation. Udio's AI music generator allegedly reproduced protected elements of existing recordings closely enough that one generated track, "Sunshine Melody," was said to match melodies, chords, and backing vocals from The Temptations' "My Girl." This is a training-data problem, meaning the unauthorised copying, if it occurred, happened before deployment, not during a user interaction. A licensing review at the training stage, of the kind the subsequent UMG settlement agreement now requires for future content, is what would have been needed to catch it.

The legal picture is layered. Universal Music Group settled and moved to a licensing partnership. Warner Music Group separately reached its own settlement and licensing arrangement with Udio. Sony Music filed a new lawsuit alleging that Udio's models were trained on more than 30,000 of its recordings, a figure a judge had previously barred Sony from adding to an earlier case. A class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed, though the court moved it from Illinois to New York. A musicians' union also filed suit over the UMG-Udio deal itself, and UMG has asked a court to dismiss that claim.

None of the lawsuits outside the UMG and WMG settlements has produced a verdict, and the allegations in the Sony case and the independent artists' class action are not established findings. Whether the training process caused the specific output similarity claimed, and how broadly that similarity extends across Udio's catalogue, remains unresolved in court.

summary:
Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused the company of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, stream and share songs. UMG chairman Lucian Grainge stated the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists and songwriters while embracing new technologies and business models. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The lawsuit originated when UMG and other major record labels accused Udio of illegally training its AI on copyrighted music. The lawsuit specifically cited The Temptations' hit "My Girl," claiming Udio's system generated a similar song called "Sunshine Melody" with matching melodies, chords and backing vocals. Udio's CEO Andrew Sanchez expressed enthusiasm about collaborating with UMG, stating the partnership will help redefine how AI supports artists and fans. This represents Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label, and artists on the new platform will be compensated for their participation.
